quests.question: ___ the evidence was conclusive, the jury reached a verdict quickly.
quests.hint: The evidence is a known, shared fact that explains the quick verdict.
quests.explanation: 'Since' is preferred when the reason is already known to both speaker and listener. The conclusive evidence is a shared fact — everyone knows it — making 'since' the most natural choice here.

quests.question: He withdrew from the race ___ he had sustained a knee injury.
quests.hint: The injury is the direct, specific cause — not a background reason.
quests.explanation: 'Because' introduces the primary direct cause. The knee injury is specifically why he withdrew. 'Because' is used for direct explanations of specific events.

quests.question: ___ time was short, the manager summarised the key points only.
quests.hint: Time being short is background context — a situational reason.
quests.explanation: 'As' introduces a background situational reason, often when the reason is less emphatic. It is the weakest of the causal conjunctions and works well here as a scene-setting clause.

quests.question: Strange ___ it may seem, the method works.
quests.hint: Only one of these fits the inverted mid-sentence pattern.
quests.explanation: 'Though' can be used in a mid-sentence inverted structure: 'adjective + though + subject + verb'. 'Although' cannot be used this way. This pattern is characteristic of formal writing.

quests.question: ___ I enjoy his films, I found this one disappointing.
quests.hint: A general positive feeling is being contrasted with a specific negative reaction.
quests.explanation: 'Although' is neutral — it introduces a concession without emphasising it. 'Even though' would also work but adds stronger emphasis. 'Although' is the most balanced choice here.

quests.question: She passed the exam ___ she had barely revised.
quests.hint: Barely revising is a dramatic obstacle — the contrast is very strong.
quests.explanation: 'Even though' is used when the contrast is particularly notable or surprising. Passing with barely any revision is remarkable — 'even though' captures that emphasis better than 'although'.

quests.question: ___ the first chapter is descriptive, the second is analytical.
quests.hint: Two parts of a text are being directly compared and contrasted.
quests.explanation: 'Whereas' is used for formal direct contrast between two parallel items. It is the preferred choice in academic writing when comparing two clearly opposing things.

quests.question: ___ he prefers working in the morning, she is more productive at night.
quests.hint: Two contrasting work habits are described — one for each person.
quests.explanation: Both 'while' and 'whereas' express contrast here, but 'while' is more common in everyday speech and slightly less formal. 'Whereas' would also be acceptable.

quests.question: ___ traditional methods focus on memorisation, modern approaches emphasise understanding.
quests.hint: Two educational philosophies are being formally contrasted.
quests.explanation: 'Whereas' is the preferred choice in academic or analytical writing when two things are directly opposed. It creates a clear parallel structure.

quests.question: No sooner had the doors opened ___ the crowd rushed in.
quests.hint: With 'no sooner', only one specific word completes the pair.
quests.explanation: 'No sooner...than' is a fixed correlative pair. Never use 'when' with 'no sooner'. The structure also requires subject-auxiliary inversion after 'no sooner'.

quests.question: Scarcely had the speech begun ___ someone's phone rang.
quests.hint: With 'scarcely', only one specific word completes the pair.
quests.explanation: 'Scarcely...when' (and 'hardly...when', 'barely...when') uses 'when', not 'than'. This distinguishes it from 'no sooner...than'.

quests.question: Hardly had I fallen asleep ___ I was woken by an alarm.
quests.hint: With 'hardly', only one specific word completes the pair.
quests.explanation: 'Hardly...when' follows the same pattern as 'scarcely...when'. Both use 'when', not 'than'. All three pairs require inverted word order after the first element.

quests.question: He saved for two years ___ he could afford a house.
quests.hint: The saving had a goal — 'he could afford' has a full subject.
quests.explanation: 'So that' is the most natural choice when the purpose clause has its own subject. 'He could afford' has 'he' as its subject, making 'so that' or 'in order that' appropriate.

quests.question: She left early ___ avoid the rush-hour traffic.
quests.hint: No second subject follows — there's an infinitive verb only.
quests.explanation: 'So as to' is followed by an infinitive (with no separate subject). When the subject of the main clause and the purpose clause is the same person, 'so as to + infinitive' is used.

quests.question: The fire doors were fitted ___ the building could be evacuated quickly.
quests.hint: A passive/formal sentence with a full subject in the purpose clause.
quests.explanation: 'In order that' is a formal alternative to 'so that'. Both require a full clause with a subject. 'In order that' is preferred in formal, official, or written documents.

quests.question: The suspect was released ___ he reported to the police daily.
quests.hint: A strict legal condition was attached to the release.
quests.explanation: 'On condition that' is used in formal, legal, or official contexts. It specifies a binding condition. The daily reporting was required for the release to stand.

quests.question: The agreement will hold ___ both parties honour its terms.
quests.hint: The agreement depends on ongoing compliance — not just a one-off condition.
quests.explanation: 'As long as' suggests an ongoing condition. The agreement remains valid for the entire duration that both parties comply — it is a continuous requirement.

quests.question: You may publish the data ___ all participants have given consent.
quests.hint: Consent is a formal prerequisite for publication.
quests.explanation: 'Provided that' introduces a condition that must be satisfied before the permission is valid. All participants consenting is the required condition.

quests.question: The policy applies ___ the employee is full-time ___ part-time.
quests.hint: The policy covers both employment types — neither is excluded.
quests.explanation: 'Whether...or' covers both possibilities equally. The policy applies in both cases: full-time and part-time. It is neutral, unlike 'either...or' which may suggest only one applies.

quests.question: I cannot confirm ___ the meeting will proceed ___ be cancelled.
quests.hint: An uncertain situation with two possible outcomes is being reported.
quests.explanation: 'Whether...or' is used in embedded questions and reported speech. 'If' can replace 'whether' in informal contexts but not before 'or'.

quests.question: ___ the forecast improves ___ not, the expedition will depart on schedule.
quests.hint: The departure is confirmed regardless of both possible weather outcomes.
quests.explanation: 'Whether or not' (or 'whether...or not') emphasises that both alternatives lead to the same result. The expedition proceeds no matter which weather outcome occurs.

quests.question: The committee found the report ___ comprehensive ___ analytically rigorous.
quests.hint: Two qualities of the report are praised with equal weight.
quests.explanation: 'Both...and' emphasises that two qualities are equally present. The report is praised for both comprehensiveness and analytical rigour.

quests.question: Not only did the policy fail to achieve its aims, ___ it caused additional problems.
quests.hint: 'Not only' requires one specific word to complete the correlative pair.
quests.explanation: 'Not only...but (also)' adds a further, often more serious point. The policy failed — and additionally it caused harm. The 'but' is essential to complete the pair.

quests.question: ___ the old method ___ the new one has produced satisfactory results so far.
quests.hint: Both approaches have been unsatisfactory — neither has worked.
quests.explanation: 'Neither...nor' excludes both items completely. Neither method has worked — both have failed to produce satisfactory results.

quests.question: The project was approved ___ the budget had been significantly reduced.
quests.hint: Budget reduction would normally prevent approval — yet it was still approved.
quests.explanation: 'Even though' highlights a surprising contrast. Budget reduction is a real obstacle, yet approval happened anyway. The 'even' emphasises the unexpectedness.

quests.question: ___ you submit your application, you will receive a confirmation email.
quests.hint: The confirmation follows at a specific moment — immediately after submitting.
quests.explanation: 'Once' means 'as soon as' or 'immediately after'. The confirmation email is triggered the moment the application is submitted.

quests.question: The data must be encrypted ___ it is transmitted over the network.
quests.hint: Encryption is a security step that must happen prior to transmission.
quests.explanation: 'Before' specifies the time sequence in a technical instruction. Encryption must occur first — transmission comes second. The order is critical.

quests.question: ___ promising the data looks, it requires further verification.
quests.hint: Even very promising data must still be verified.
quests.explanation: 'However promising' means 'no matter how promising'. The word 'however' here acts as a concessive conjunction meaning 'to whatever extent'. Verification is required regardless of how good the data looks.

quests.question: She agreed to the terms, ___ she was not entirely satisfied with them.
quests.hint: Agreeing despite dissatisfaction is a surprising combination.
quests.explanation: 'Even though' introduces a factual concession. She was genuinely dissatisfied — yet she still agreed. The 'even' signals how notable the contrast is.

quests.question: The system failed ___ a critical update had not been installed.
quests.hint: The missing update is the direct technical reason for the failure.
quests.explanation: 'Because' introduces the direct cause of the system failure. The missing update is specifically why the system failed.
